lines: There goes the first lamp. The rest follow like good colleagues.
Lamps on, one by one down the promenade. Like a slow sentence.
Lamp by lamp. I try to guess which one is next. Wrong again.
Lamps on. At home in winter they never get a night off.
The lamp by the kiosk is always fashionably late.
Click, glow. Click, glow. The promenade is counting.
Lamps on. That is my cue to stop calling it afternoon.
Each lamp comes on a bit orange, then thinks better of it.
Somebody up there has a very gentle switch.
Lamps on, sea still pink. The overlap is my favourite minute.
Lyktene er tent. The lamps are lit. Cosier in Norwegian.
A lamp just came on above a gull. He did not look impressed.
The lamps never hurry. I am taking notes.
Through the window the lamps go out. The sea takes over.
Lamps out. The day has the promenade now. I join it at eight.
Lamps off, just as the kettle clicks. Teamwork.
Sun over the hill. It finds my desk before I do.
Sun up behind the hill. The curtains have gone apricot.
Soloppgang. Sunrise. I see it best with one eye still shut.
The sun is up over the hill. Good. One of us should be.
There it goes. The sun is dipping a toe in the bay.
Sun on the water. Everyone at the railing just went quiet.
Sun meets sea. Every evening, and nobody is ever late.
Half a sun now. I always think it slows down at the end.
Solnedgang. At home in June it barely bothers. Here, a show.
Sunset. My shadow reaches all the way to the café.
The last bit of sun. A small orange full stop.
I clap a little, inside. Same as everyone else here.
Watching the sun set with strangers. By the end, not strangers.
The bay takes the sun without a sound. Very polite bay.
The sun just laid a gold road on the water. Straight to me.
The sun is going down exactly where Odile said it would.
First star. Over the bay, right where the sun went.
One star. Then two. Then I lost count, happily.
Same stars as at home. They just get here warmer.
A star came out above the workshop. The builder will not notice.
Stjerner. The first ones. I like them before they crowd in.
The stars are early tonight. Or I am late.
A star, then a plane pretending to be a star. Then a real one.
That one is Venus, I think. Henri says it is a lamp. Either way.
First star. The lamps look a bit shy now.
Enough stars now to call it night. Officially.
The moon over the bay. It laid a silver path to my bench.
Moon's up. The sea looks freshly ironed.
Månen. Same moon as at home. It looks more relaxed here.
The moon is up. The gulls have gone to bed. Sensible.
Moon up. Even the fountain seems to be whispering.
From my desk window: a moon, a bay. Nothing else needed.
The moon is up. Biscuit once barked at it. Once.
Half a moon tonight. The other half is probably at home.
The moon makes the white houses look like paper lanterns.
{name}'s window just came on. Welcome home, {name}.
There, {name}'s light. Now the street feels complete.
{name} is in. Kitchen light first, as always.
Lys i vinduet. {name} is home. Good.
A yellow square up the street. That will be {name}.
{name} just switched the light on. Kettle next, I bet.
Hei, {name}. I can see your lamp from my bench.
{name}'s window on, mine still dark. I am late home again.
{name} is home. Curtain half drawn. Very sensible.
Sov godt, {name}. Your window just said goodnight.
{name} has gone to bed. Sensible. I have three more minutes.
{name}'s light is out. The street is down to the lamps and me.
One window fewer. {name} is asleep. I lower my voice.
{name} turned in. I take that as a hint and head home.
From my window I see {name}'s go dark. Mine next, soon.
{name}'s window is dark. An early night. Good for {name}.
Lights out at {name}'s. The cat on the sill stays up.
Eight bells from the old town. Marcel is already pouring.
The church bell. Eight. My coffee says I have time.
Eight o'clock, says the bell. Croissant o'clock, says me.
The bell up the hill. Far off, like someone else's alarm.
Noon bell from the old town. The baguette agrees.
Kirkeklokka. The bell at home sounds deeper. This one smiles.
The bell rings noon and every shutter seems to yawn.
Six from the church. The day is officially off duty.
The church bell at six. Somewhere a pot goes on a stove.
The bell up in the old town. Soft, as if checking we are up.
Every chair taken. I am guarding mine with one elbow.
Marcel is carrying four cups and a conversation. Impressive.
Full terrace before nine. The town runs on crème.
Cups on saucers all round me. Like a room of small typewriters.
A table of six sharing one newspaper. Section by section.
Lunch rush. I will eat my baguette on the move. Very local.
The terrace is full and Marcel is somehow at every table.
Henri and Odile at their table. The tarte has arrived.
From the bench I hear six languages and one laugh. Henri's.
The terrace is full. Every candle has a face beside it.
The café has reached the loud, happy part of the evening.
Marcel just did a full lap with a tray. Not one olive lost.
Rosé on every table. Golden hour is very well organised here.
A café this full, up north, would make the evening news.
No window seat today. The window will cope without me.
Three o'clock. The café is just Marcel and the parasols.
Empty terrace. Every chair facing the sea, waiting politely.
The quiet hour. Even the sugar bowls look sleepy.
One cup on one table. Somebody had the whole place to themselves.
Café is empty. I could bring the builder a coffee. Or two.
A sparrow is checking every table for crumbs. Thorough work.
Stille på kafeen. Marcel is polishing a glass that was clean.
Marcel is unfolding the parasols. The day is officially on.
Chairs going out, one by one. I could set a clock by him.
Cloths on the tables. Mine is the one by the window.
The parasols open like they are yawning. Same, honestly.
Chairs going up on the tables. The café says god natt.
Marcel stacks the last chairs. Even the clatter is gentle.
Last table cleared. Tomorrow I plan to be its first customer.
The terrace folds itself away. Same time tomorrow, café.
There goes the accordion. My foot has started without me.
First couple out. Camille and Théo, always the brave ones.
Music under the string lights. The evening has changed gear.
First song. Everyone pretends not to want to dance. For now.
Lucie said she would not dance. The music has other plans.
Music. Henri just straightened his collar. Something is coming.
Opening song. I know this one. I do not know the steps.
Musikk! Right on time, as if the lamps had told it.
Camille leads, Théo follows. Very good arrangement.
I am dancing on the inside. Mostly from the knees down.
The accordion speeds up. Everyone spins a little wider.
Someone just dipped someone. The whole square said ooh.
Tapping the bench in time. The bench seems to approve.
Shadows dancing on the café wall too. Twice the dancers.
A slow song now. The square goes all soft at the edges.
At home we dance round the Christmas tree. This is warmer.
Théo asked if I would join. I said next song. Every song.
Every time the accordion turns, someone new gets up. Not me. Yet.
A little crowd at the railing. We all shuffle up to make room.
Shoulder to shoulder at the railing. Nobody talks. Lovely.
Biscuit has the best spot. Front row, nose through the rails.
Same faces every evening. The sunset club. No membership card.
Someone said 'there it goes'. Everyone else said it a beat later.
The builder came out too. Ten minutes, he said. Twelve, I bet.
Everyone leaning the same way. The railing must feel popular.
Nobody planned to meet here. Everybody did anyway.
A row of people and a row of gulls. All watching the sun.
Up north this would need jackets. Here, only company.
The crowd goes quiet for the last bit. Like a cinema.
I made room for a visitor. She said merci. I said bare hyggelig.
Crowd at the railing already. I am late to my own habit.
A radio from Henri and Odile's window. Morning news, very gently.
The morning programme drifts across. I catch every fifth word.
Henri's radio. A weather report that is mostly the word soleil.
The radio over the street and the café spoons keep one beat.
A radio from the family's window. An old song for the sunset.
Radio from an open window. The singer sounds like she means it.
An old song from a window. Mormor had this one on a record.
A radio jingle from upstairs. It lives in my head now. Fine.
A radio up there, the sea down here. Decent duet.
The kiosk shutter rattles down. Postcards off to bed.
Hei, {name}. Same time as yesterday. We are reliable people.
{name} waved with a whole arm. I only managed a hand. Next time.
There goes {name}, walking like someone with a good plan.
God morgen, {name}! Or bonjour. Whichever lands first.
{name} said bonjour, I said hei. We met in the middle.
{name} went by humming. Now I am humming it too.
{name} nodded at me like we share a secret. Probably the weather.
Hei, {name}! I owe you a coffee. Or you owe me. One of those.
{name} walks faster than me. I have made my peace with it.
Ha det, {name}. It means see you. It sounds like a sneeze.
Kveld, {name}. That is evening. Mostly I just say hei.
{name} and I have said hei about a thousand times. Still nice.
{name} says the lamps come on soon. Takk for tipset.
Natta, {name}. Sleep well, when you get there.
{name} went past and leaned on the railing too. Good instinct.
{name} peeked at my coffee. Marcel's. Very black. Approved.
Lucie and a baguette, flat out. The baguette looks thrilled.
Lucie waved without letting go. Very advanced cycling.
Lucie shouted 'kiosk later!' over her shoulder. Yes. Always.
Lucie has the wind at her back today. I can tell by the grin.
Lucie rode past standing on the pedals. Show-off. Lovely.
Lucie's scarf went past about a second after Lucie did.
Lucie gave me a nod and a wobble. Mostly nod.
Lucie flew past the terrace. Marcel lifted a cup at her anyway.
Inès went by counting under her breath. I lost count for her.
Hei, Inès! She held up four fingers. Lap four, I think.
Inès ran past my coffee. The steam is still catching up.
Inès is racing the sunset again. I am cheering for Inès.
Inès asked 'one lap?' and was gone before I said i morgen.
Inès, this is my full speed. Truly. This is it.
Inès gave me a thumbs-up for walking. Very generous coach.
Inès runs like the promenade slopes downhill. Both ways.
Biscuit went by with Yusuf in tow. Clear who walks whom.
Hei, Biscuit. One sniff of my shoelace. Approved, I think.
Biscuit paused at my chair. Yusuf said no croissant. Fair.
Yusuf's lantern and Biscuit's tail, bobbing in time.
My downstairs neighbours just went by. One of them has a tail.
Biscuit on official business. Every lamp post, inspected.
Yusuf nodded. Biscuit nodded harder. With the whole dog.
God kveld, Biscuit. God kveld, Yusuf. In order of wag.
Biscuit turned round when I said hei. He speaks Norwegian now.
Biscuit glanced at the sunset, then at me. Then back. Critic.
Night round. Biscuit stopped at my bench for one exact second.
Léo! How many laps? He held up both hands and a foot.
Léo shot past shouting a number. Lap eleven, I hope.
Léo is faster than last week. He will tell me so in a minute.
Léo overtook me and said 'beat you'. I did not know we raced.
There goes Léo, arms out like a plane. Very low-flying.
Léo asked me to time him. I counted 'fast'. He was pleased.
Henri and Odile, arm in arm. Same pace for forty-one years.
Odile waved, Henri nodded. They split the greeting duties.
Henri and Odile walk slower than the shadows. Very wise.
Henri pointed at the sea. Odile said yes, darling, the sea.
Henri and Odile. I would like to walk like that one day.
Odile fixed my collar in passing. She did not even stop.
Henri said 'young man' and walked on. A full conversation.
Lucie's bell. Two rings is hello. One ring is 'move, Asgeir'.
Ding-ding. I stepped aside before I even looked. Trained.
Lucie's bell sounds like a very small church. Morning service.
A bell behind me. Lucie, or the town's smallest tram.
Lucie rang at a gull. The gull stayed put. Lucie went round.
The bell got here before Lucie did. A small herald.
The bell, and every cup on the terrace lifted a little.
A gull out over the water. Sounds like it found something good.
That gull sounds just like the gulls at home. Hei, cousin.
A gull called. Another answered from far off. Long distance.
One gull, one call, and the sea suddenly feels bigger.
A gull just said its piece. Fair point, probably.
Gull on duty out there. I raise my coffee to it.
That gull call means lunch somewhere. Hopefully not mine.
The gull has thoughts about the workshop. Loud, positive ones.
A gull outside the post office. Even the birds send messages.
Inès is at the next table, already done with a whole lap of the day.
Inès eats her croissant in three bites. Efficient, even here.
Inès has her emails open and her croissant first. Correct order.
Inès, walking and typing. "Five minutes," she says. It will be.
There goes Inès. I wave, she counts the wave as a lap.
Inès is at the railing, finally standing still. Rare sight.
Inès is saying "wait for it" to the sun. The sun is waiting.
Inès has one glass of rosé and both feet already tapping.
Marcel carries six cups and a smile. I could carry one.
Marcel brings table four its sea view. They all want it.
Marcel, arms folded by the door. The quiet hour suits him.
Marcel has the rosé tray. Golden hour, as he predicted.
Marcel, still on his feet. I think he is part tray by now.
Marcel spins round a pram with a tray. Ten out of ten.
Henri is watering the lemons. They look ready to say thanks.
Henri lifts the can like a teapot. Very polite watering.
Henri is reading the paper out loud. Odile pretends not to listen.
Henri has the crossword and the pencil. Odile has the answers.
Henri, small strong coffee. Marcel knows not to ask.
Henri is pointing out windows as they light. A good job to have.
Henri raises a glass to forty-one years. I raise a hand. Skål.
Odile is waving me over. I will learn something either way.
Odile solved "soir" before Henri finished reading the clue.
Odile has Henri's arm and his hat. She is in charge of both.
Odile is watching the evening like a theatre. Front row.
Odile ordered the tarte. Marcel brought two forks. He knows.
Odile says half a glass. Marcel pours exactly half. Diplomacy.
Yusuf and Biscuit. Biscuit is navigating, Yusuf is crew.
Yusuf is on the long evening round. Biscuit chose it.
Yusuf has Biscuit sitting for the sunset. Better manners than me.
Yusuf is describing the sky to his mum. She is getting details.
Yusuf's lantern going round the promenade. Like a small moon.
Biscuit is pulling towards the fountain. Yusuf says nei.
Biscuit is staring at a sandwich. Pure focus. I could learn.
Biscuit is sitting nicely and watching the sea. Good dog. Flink.
Biscuit in the lantern light. Little shadow, very big tail.
Lucie on her rounds. She is faster than the gulls before nine.
Lucie, rosé, obviously. She raises it at me. Skål, Lucie.
Lucie is pointing at the last pink bit. I see it. Just.
Léo is on lap nine round the fountain. I am out of breath for him.
Léo just shouted "bet you cannot catch me". Correct, Léo.
Léo is counting coins in the fountain. He will report back.
Léo has his nose an inch from the water. Very serious science.
Léo is sitting very straight for his citron pressé.
Léo is practising for tonight. Mostly the jumping part.
Léo is waving goodbye to the sun. Very thorough goodbye.
Léo is negotiating five more minutes. Strong case, I thought.
Camille, phone in hand, eyes on Léo. Two jobs at once.
Camille just said "not in the fountain". Léo heard "fountain".
Camille ordered the salade niçoise. It looks like a painting.
Camille is peering at the arcade. Go on in, I want to say.
Camille at the railing, everything gold. She said so. True.
Camille is steering Léo home. He is steering back.
Camille has a glass at last. Léo is asleep. Well earned.
Camille, dancing, reminding Théo of a promise. He is keeping it.
Théo has two baguettes. One will not make it home.
Théo is telling his table the post office does robot mail. Close.
Théo is choosing between rosé and pastis. It will be rosé.
Théo is calling Camille to come and see. She already sees it.
Théo is toasting sleeping children. I toast them too.
Théo, dancing, says he never promised. His feet did.
The builder is bent over the bench. Tongue out. Good sign.
The builder is humming through the window. Something works.
The builder's light is still on. One more commit, he says.
The builder is on the terrace, explaining Toolrails to a croissant.
The builder is outside the arcade, grinning at his phone.
The builder is in the doorway: come back tomorrow, it says.
The builder, leaning on the rail, deploys on pause. Bra.
Marcel says "yes, we have olives" before anyone asks.
Henri, strolling slowly. The sun is not going anywhere, he says.
Odile has spotted me. I will be told who everyone is.
Léo is doing laps again. His friend is a lap behind. Always.
Camille is having a slow wander. No phone. Good afternoon for it.
Théo is sniffing his baguette. Still warm. He nods at me.
Théo is leaning on the rail like a postcard of himself.
The builder is back in. "Back to it," and the radio goes on.
Camille and Théo, clinking. The evening is theirs now.
Henri folded the newspaper into a hat. For the sun, he says.
The fountain says the same thing all day. Never boring.
Somebody wished on a krone. Long way from home, that coin.
Pigeons queueing at the rim. Very orderly. Very Norwegian.
Dipped a finger in the fountain. Colder than it looks. Good.
Small rainbow in the spray. The fountain showing off a bit.
Pappa had a fountain story. I only remember the splash part.
A sparrow bathing in the fountain. Full spa treatment.
I tossed a coin in once. Wished for good coffee. Got Marcel.
I can hear the fountain from this bench. Steady as a clock.
Léo is lapping the fountain. I am lapping the promenade. Fair.
Léo just overtook his friend on the corner. Clean move.
Lap nine, maybe ten. Léo's counting is generous.
Two boys, one fountain, no finish line. Perfect race.
Hei, Léo! Wide on the bend, tight on the straight.
I would race him. I would also lose. Better to cheer.
His friend says Léo cut the corner. Léo says it is round.
Léo shouts the lap count. The whole square keeps score now.
Somebody should paint a start line. Léo would ignore it.
Postcards on the spinner. I always buy the one with lemons.
The kiosk cup is small and hot. Exactly the right size of break.
The newspapers flap on their clips. Like a tiny laundry line.
Elbows on the kiosk counter, coffee in hand, no rush at all.
A postcard for Mamma. I will write it here. The sea will help.
They have one bar of Norwegian chocolate here. I let it be.
Gulls on the kiosk roof, reading over my shoulder.
Sugar cubes in a jar on the counter. Very civilised.
From the kiosk I can see the whole promenade. Nice to check.
The kiosk lights its one bulb. Cosiest corner of the evening.
Morning at the post office. The sorting never stopped.
The post office sign has a soft hum. It keeps good time.
Late, and the post office is still lit. It always waits up.
Checking the post. Mostly I check the view behind it.
The builder checked the post just before me. Early bird.
Post office window glowing blue. A nightlight for the square.
Odile calls it the post office that forgot to close. Fair.
The post office in this light looks like a stamp of itself.
The arcade marquee just woke up. Lights chasing each other.
The marquee bulbs run left to right. I always follow them once.
Giggling from inside the arcade. Somebody found a good blank.
Fun Libs has an arcade now. Seventeen-year-old me would grin.
The arcade looks sleepy in daylight. Saving itself for later.
Someone wrote 'a damp sock' into a story. I heard the laugh.
Arcade lights on the tiles by the fountain. Double marquee.
Never put up a poster for the arcade. People find it anyway.
From here the arcade blinks like it is telling a long joke.
One bulb on the marquee is a little slow. My favourite one.
Léo's friend reads the stories out loud. Dramatic pauses.
He has a new whiteboard. Mostly arrows. Good arrows.
The workshop smells of coffee and warm laptop. Promising.
He held up four fingers. Four connectors. I gave a thumb.
Workshop lights still on. The builder and the moths agree.
He talks to the screen in there. The screen seems to listen.
Every tool on one wall in there. Fitting, really.
The door is ajar. I stay outside. You do not interrupt flow.
His tea went cold on the windowsill. Sign of a good afternoon.
Chalk on the workshop step: a little arrow pointing in.
Tool search, he says. Find me the sugar, I say. He laughs.
The library is resting. One lamp on, like a bookmark.
That reading lamp in the library window. I check on it nightly.
Library doors shut, chairs tucked in. It is taking a breather.
The library lamp is a promise. A small one, but kept.
The library steps are warm. Good place to sit and not read.
Sun across the library windows. All the spines go gold.
A cat on the library step. Head librarian, for now.
The library lamp drops one yellow square on the pavement.
Dust in the library window light. Resting, but it looks busy.
The library lamp and the evening star. Both on early.
Elbows on the warm rail, sea in front. Ferdig for i dag.
Blue hour on the water. Hard to tell where the sea stops.
From the bench the sea is just a sound now. A good one.
The sea up north is grey and serious. This one is cheerful.
Little waves arriving in no particular order. Restful.
The sea breeze parts my hair somewhere new every time.
I came to think about work. The sea talked me out of it.
Waves on the stones below the bench. Slow applause.
Noon glitter on the water. Too bright to look at. I look.
The horizon is gone. Just a soft line I am imagining.
Henri's bench faces the sea. Of course it does.
Shoes on. Marcel will have the window seat wiped by now.
One email, then the café. Fine, two emails, then the café.
Practising my bonjour on the stairs. Marcel deserves a good one.
Out the door before the croissants are all spoken for.
The café chairs are out. My cue to find my shoes.
Last sip, then the post office. It has been open all night anyway.
Post office next, to see who wrote overnight.
Finishing the croissant on the walk. The pigeons will follow.
Après le café, la poste. Marcel taught me that, roughly.
Right. The desk is calling. It calls very politely.
Back up the stairs. Window open first, then the laptop.
Desk time soon. I have three good ideas from the walk here.
Desk in five minutes. Today's list fits on one sticky note.
Save, close, stand up. Henri promised a crossword clue at eleven.
Ten more minutes at the desk, then I go ask after the lemons.
Nearly eleven. Bench o'clock. Henri keeps the time better than me.
Sun is down. A bench next, for the windows coming on.
One more look at the water, then a bench and the evening lamps.
Moving to the bench soon. The lit windows are the second show.
Henri, I am off for bread. The warm kind, if Théo is not first.
Time for a little wander. Baguette first, direction later.
Bread run next. Théo says the noon batch is the best one.
Empty cup, full head. Time to wander until the light turns gold.
Cup in the bin, then a slow walk. No route. That is the plan.
Kiosk done. Now a wander with no destination. Very continental.
Baguette is still warm. If I hurry home, it stays that way.
Lunch at the desk soon. Bread, cheese, and a window full of sea.
In ten minutes I knock on the workshop window. He expects it.
Closing the laptop. Time to see what the builder made since lunch.
Workshop visit next. I am bringing questions and no tools.
Packing a biscuit for the builder. He forgets to eat on good days.
One wave goodbye through the glass, then a lap of the promenade.
I will walk this over. Tool search makes sense at walking pace.
Off for a loop soon. The thinking happens around the fountain.
Leaving the workshop to its humming. My legs want a loop.
One more stretch of promenade, then kiosk coffee. Lucie's orders.
I can see the kiosk from here. Coffee in about four minutes.
Half a lap to go. The kiosk coffee is the reward.
Heading to the railing soon. My spot is by the third lamp.
Sunset in an hour. I like to get to the railing early.
Railing next. The builder said he would join for ten minutes.
Turning toward the sea now. The sky is starting its warm-up.
A few more lit windows, then mine. Mine goes on last tonight.
Bedtime soon. Up north it is still bright. Here I get stars.
Home in a moment. I will say god natt to the fountain on the way.
Ten more minutes on this bench, then the stairs, then god natt.
The post office sign just brightened. Somebody's agent wrote home.
There it goes. An agent sent a letter. I did not even see a stamp.
The post office just blinked. An agent working late. Kindly.
Right on cue. The sign flares while I lean on the postbox.
Another email handled. Nobody licked an envelope. Remarkable.
The sign glows a bit brighter. Somewhere an inbox got tidier.
Lys i posten. Light in the post office. An agent on duty.
The post office flared. Marcel thought it was the sun. Fair.
An agent just replied to someone. Probably more politely than me.
About a hundred providers, one little sign. It just flickered.
The post office lit up behind me. The sun has competition.
Seventeen tools behind that glow. Tonight it needed one.
Walking past just as the sign flares. Like a wave hello.
Henri asked who writes all that post. Agents, I said. Hat tipped.
The sign brightens. The gull on the roof does not even blink.
I wonder what that one said. Probably: thank you, see attached.
Before my second coffee, an agent has sent a letter. Impressive.
From the bench I see the post office blink. Mail, delivered.
The post office flared across the way. The builder looked up too.
Kiosk coffee, and over there the post office winks. Good timing.
The arcade sign flared. Somebody just filled in a silly word.
Someone just played Fun Libs. I hope they picked a ridiculous noun.
A story got finished somewhere. The arcade blinks to say so.
Marquee chasing, sign flaring. Someone wrote a funny one tonight.
The arcade lit up as I passed. Adjective, noun, a big laugh.
Léo would want to know which word they chose. So do I, honestly.
The workshop sign flared. An agent found the right tool. Bra.
Toolrails just did its thing. One URL, and the agent found a tool.
Sign is brighter. The builder pretends not to grin. He grins.
An agent borrowed a tool next door. Put it back neatly, I hope.
Workshop sign just brightened. Toolrails is awake, like the builder.
There they go. One lamp, then the next, all the way to the kiosk.
Lamps on. In a Norwegian June we would wait until August for this.
Each lamp hums a little as it wakes. You hear it if you stand close.
The lamps and the sea turned orange at once. Coordinated.
Lamp by lamp, the promenade draws itself a dotted line.
The lamp outside just clicked off. My new alarm clock.
Sunrise from the kitchen. The hill goes pink, then the roofs.
Up with the sun for once. Do not tell Inès. She will make it a rule.
There, it touches. I always want to say: careful, the sea is wet.
Half a sun left. I am not blinking.
The sun is in the sea. Someone should write this down. Not me.
Mormor called this the sun tucking itself in. Good night, sun.
I lean a little to the left, as if that helps it land.
Down it goes into the bay. Ten points for a clean entry.
First star, right over the library roof. God kveld to you.
There is the first star. I wish for another day like this one.
Two stars now. Three. Like guests, they arrive politely late.
Stars over the old town. The church tower points at one of them.
I know one constellation. I will sit here until it turns up.
Walking home by moonlight. The cobbles have silver edges.
A big moon tonight. The fountain has a small wobbly one too.
{name}'s window just came on. I am learning everyone's light.
